Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[0].Custom_Phase.#text: Implementation & Physical Design
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[0].Description.xhtml:p: Establish and enforce HDL coding and review
			practices that minimize differences between simulation
			semantics and synthesis interpretation. Avoid HDL
			constructs, synthesis directives, and tool-dependent
			behaviors known to cause simulation/synthesis mismatch,
			with particular attention to security-relevant
			logic.
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[0].Effectiveness: High
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[0].Effectiveness_Notes.xhtml:p: Avoidance of the patterns of code which can
			result in these errors removes the opportunity for
			error. However, in some cases (notably state machine
			encodings) this can be very difficult to achieve
			efficiently.
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[1].Custom_Phase.@Domain: Hardware
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[1].Custom_Phase.#text: Implementation & Physical Design
Potential_Mi

tigations.Mitigation[1].Description.xhtml:p: For security-critical logic, preserve intentional
			redundancy that is required for security. Examples may
			include redundant logic, triple modular redundancy (TMR)
			structures, Hamming-distance state encodings, or
			state-machine recovery logic. Use synthesis constraints,
			preservation attributes, carefully controlled structural
			implementation, or manual implementation of selected
			critical blocks to prevent this redundancy from being
			merged, re-encoded, or optimized away.
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[1].Effectiveness: High
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[1].Effectiveness_Notes.xhtml:p: This mitigation removes the structures which
			cause the problem, at the expense of additional design and
			verification effort, and additional risk of inclusion of
			other functional errors.

Demonstrative_Examples.Demonstrative_Example[0].Example_Code[2].xhtml:p: For combinational logic, ensure that simulation is

Demonstrative_Examples.Demonstrative_Example[0].Body_Text[1].xhtml:p: The always block is intended to describe
			combinational logic for unlocked_next, which depends on
			four sig

nals (lock, unlock, unlocked and reset). However,
			the sensitivity list is missing reset., During pre-synthesis RTL simulation, this tells
			the simulator not to rerun the block when reset changes
			(only when the other signals change). The signal
			unlocked_next defaults to 1’b0 so the simulation sees the
			expected locked state and so the tests of the state after
			reset will pass., Synthesis tools assume a complete sensitivity
			list and will therefore infer logic including the reset
			signal. When reset is high, the unlocked _next signal is
			(erroneously) set to 1’b1. This is a bug (as reset should
			force a non-unlocked state), which would be expected to be
			found in simulation. The design uses a two-process state
			machine style which masks this bug in the code during
			simulation, but allows it to propagate to the synthesized
			implementation.
Demonstrative_Examples.Demonstrative_Example[0].Body_Text[2].xhtml:p: The synthesized hardware exits reset in an
			insecure state (with unlocked set to 1’b1) and remains in
			that state until one of the lock/unlock signals changes
			state. An adversary can take advantage of this by
			exploiting whatever logic makes use of this signal to set
			itself to a secure state.

Demonstrative_Examples.Demonstrative_Example[1].Body_Text[0].xhtml:p: The design assigns the security-relevant secure
			signal using logic that is hidden from synthesis by
			translate_off / translate_on or equivalent synthesis
			exclusion directives. Simulation tools treat these
			directives as comments and include the enclosed
			assignment, so simulation updates secure according to
			security_check(policy_ok, lock_ready) and appears to
			validate the intended protected-mode behavior., Synthesis tools omit the code between the
			exclusion directives. The synthesized implementation
			therefore does not contain the same assignment that was
			exercised during simulation. This creates a
			simulation/synthesis mismatch in security-relevant
			behavior: the HDL model used for verification enables or
			disables protected mode using logic that is absent from
			the synthesized hardware.
Demonstrative_Examples.Demonstrative_Example[1].Body_Text[1].xhtml:p: Because the synthesized implementation does not
			include the same logic that was present during simulation,
			the hardware defaults to an insecure state. An attacker
			can take advantage of this to execute activities which
			would normally require some form of authorization, even
			though simulation results suggested that protected mode
			would be enforced.

Demonstrative_Examples.Demonstrative_Example[2].Example_Code[2].xhtml:p: Do not rely on a VHDL others choice or Verilog default
			  branch to guarantee post-synthesis recovery behavior for
			  security-critical state machines. If recovery from
			  unexpected state encodings affects access to protected
			  configuration registers, the implementation should not
			  depend on synthesis inferring and preserving that
			  behavior from RTL alone., For this type of security-critical controller, implement
			  the state machine using a carefully-controlled
			  structural or hand-synthesized representation where the
			  relevant state elements, reset behavior, transition
			  logic, and fail-closed recovery behavior are
			  explicit. Be careful that the synthesiser does not infer
			  a state machine from the crafted lo

gic, and “undo” the
			  work. Review the resulting gate-level or structural
			  implementation to confirm that unintended encodings are
			  handled as required., Perform post-synthesis simulations where faults are
			  injected into the state registers and confirm the
			  behavior., Perform formal analysis to prove that the behavior of
			  these critical blocks has not been altered by the
			  synthesis process., After the implementation is verified and validated,
			  preserve it during integration so later synthesis or
			  whole-design optimization does not re-encode, merge,
			  remove, or otherwise transform the security-critical
			  recovery logic., This approach is costly and design-specific, but it is
			  appropriate when relying on ordinary RTL synthesis would
			  create unacceptable security risk.
Demonstrative_Examples.Demonstrative_Example[2].Body_Text[0].xhtml:p: The design relies on a VHDL others choice or
			Verilog default branch to express recovery behavior for
			state values not explicitly listed in the state transition
			logic. In RTL simulation, the intended behavior is that
			unexpected controller states will transition to USER_ONLY,
			where protected configuration writes are
			blocked., The error is assuming that this RTL-level
			recovery behavior will necessarily be preserved after
			synthesis. During synthesis, the state machine may be
			encoded, optimized, or transformed based on the states
			considered reachable during normal operation. As a result,
			logic associated with unused or faulty hardware encodings
			may be removed or altered, and the synthesized
			implementation may not preserve the same recovery behavior
			that appeared in RTL simulation.
Demonstrative_Examples.Demonstrative_Example[2].Body_Text[1].xhtml:p: If t

he synthesized implementation does not
			preserve the unexpected-state recovery behavior, the
			hardware may fail to return to USER_ONLY after a fault,
			reset anomaly, voltage glitch, clock disturbance, or other
			condition that places the state storage into an unintended
			encoding., An attacker who can induce or influence such
			conditions may be able to leave protected configuration
			writes enabled, or cause them to become enabled, even
			though simulation suggested that unexpected state values
			would be forced into a state where those writes are
			blocked.

@Name: Insufficient Session Timeout Value
@Abstraction: Base
@Structure: Simple
@Status: Incomplete
Description: The product establishes an authenticated user session, but it does not properly set a timeout for the session. That is, the timeout is set to an excessively large value or is not set at all.
Technical_Nuance.xhtml:p: There are two types of session timeouts.
Technical_Nuance.xhtml:ul.xhtml:li: Inactivity Timeout: The time window that a session will be expired if there is no user interaction within the session., Absolute Timeout: Regardless of activity, the total lifetime of a session before it is forcefully expired.

Common_Consequences.Consequence.Scope: Access Control, Integrity
Common_Consequences.Consequence.Impact: Gain Privileges or Assume Identity
Common_Consequences.Consequence.Note.xhtml:p: This weakness may improve the likely success of
	      certain attacks. For example, an attacker

may intercept
	      a session ID, possibly via a network sniffer or
	      Cross-site Scripting attack. Although short session
	      expiration times do not help if a stolen token is
	      immediately used, they will protect against ongoing
		replaying of the session ID., In another scenario, a user might access a web site
		  from a shared computer (such as at a library,
		  Internet cafe, or open work environment), but forget
		  to close the pages before leaving. A long expiration
		  could allow an attacker to use the browser's back
		  button to access web pages previously accessed by
		  the victim.
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[0].Phase: Implementation
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[0].Description: Ensure that user sessions have appropriate absolute timeouts set. The industry standard is between 4 and 8 hours for an absolute timeout [REF-1540].
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[1].Phase: Implementation
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[1].Description: Ensure that user sessions have appropriate inactivity timeouts set. 2 to 5 minutes is recommended for high-value applications, and 15-30 minutes for low-risk applications [REF-1540].
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[2].Phase: Implementation
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[2].Description: If using an authentication token for a user session, ensure that the token lifetime is configured based on the recommended best practices from the token provider [REF-1563]. There are situations using authentication tokens such as a JWT (Java Web Token) in which the server-side does not handle session timeouts and trusts the values directly from the token. In this case, it is important that the timeout value is set correctly for the token that is granted.

Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[0].Description: Developers should anticipate that terminators will be injected/removed/manipulated in the input vectors of their product. Use an appropriate combination of denylists and allowlists to ensure only valid, expected and appropriate input is processed by the system.
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[1].@Mitigation_ID: MIT-5
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[1].Phase: Implementation
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[1].Strategy: Input Validation
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[1].Description.xhtml:p: Assume all input is malicious. Use an "accept known good" input validation strategy, i.e., use a list of acceptable inputs that strictly conform to specifications. Reject any input that does not strictly

conform to specifications, or transform it into something that does., When performing input validation, consider all potentially relevant properties, including length, type of input, the full range of acceptable values, missing or extra inputs, syntax, consistency across related fields, and conformance to business rules. As an example of business rule logic, "boat" may be syntactically valid because it only contains alphanumeric characters, but it is not valid if the input is only expected to contain colors such as "red" or "blue.", Do not rely exclusively on looking for malicious or malformed inputs. This is likely to miss at least one undesirable input, especially if the code's environment changes. This can give attackers enough room to bypass the intended validation. However, denylists can be useful for detecting potential attacks or determining which inputs are so malformed that they should be rejected outright.
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[2].@Mitigation_ID: MIT-28
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[2].Phase: Implementation
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[2].Strategy: Output Encoding
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[2].Description: While it is risky to use dynamically-generated query strings, code, or commands that mix control and data together, sometimes it may be unavoidable. Properly quote arguments and escape any special characters within those arguments. The most conservative approach is to escape or filter all characters that do not pass an extremely strict allowlist (such as everything that is not alphanumeric or white space). If some special characters are still needed, such as white space, wrap each argument in quotes after the escaping/filtering step. Be careful of argument injection (CWE-88).
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[3].@Mitigation_ID: MIT-20

Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[3].Phase: Implementation
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[3].Strategy: Input Validation
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[3].Description: Inputs should be decoded and canonicalized to the application's current internal representation before being validated (CWE-180). Make sure that the application does not decode the same input twice (CWE-174). Such errors could be used to bypass allowlist validation schemes by introducing dangerous inputs after they have been checked.

@ID: 1476
@Name: Improper Request Propagation before Data Reception in Write Transactions in a Bus Architecture
@Abstraction: Base
@Structure: Simple
@Status: Incomplete
Description: The product uses a multi-manager shared bus architecture
	    with an on-chip interconnect that speculatively propagates
	    a request for a write transaction, but it does not ensure
	    that the remaining steps required by the manager module to
	    complete the request are fulfilled in a timely manner.
Technical_Nuance: Here, the word "speculatively" refers to the fact that the
	    interconnect propagates the request assuming that the
	    manager will at some point provide the data, thus
	    releasing the use of the bus.

hnology[2].@Class: System on Chip
Applicable_Platforms.Technology[2].@Prevalence: Undetermined
Background_Details.Background_Detail.xhtml:p: Some products may use an architecture with a
	      shared bus that is accessible by multiple devices, in
	      which these devices can issue requests that utilize the
	      shared bus. There may be an on-chip interconnect based
	      on a protocol that manages the devices' requests to the
	      bus and enforces the ordering of requests and data. When
	      a device makes a request, the bus might indefinitely
	      lock the write access to a shared output link until the
	      initiating device finishes its transaction. If the
	      initiating device does not finish the transaction
	      quickly enough, this can prevent other devices from
	      using the bus, causing a denial of service., A "manager module" is a hardware component that
	      initiates transactions on the interconnect, such as a
	      processor, DMA engine, or hardware
	      accelerator.
Modes_Of_Introduction.Introduction.Custom_Phase.@Domain: Hardware
Modes_Of_Introduction.Introduction.Custom_Phase.#text: Hardware Requirements
Modes_Of_Introduction.Introduction.Note.xhtml:p: This occurs if the on-chip communication
		interconnect is based on a multi-channel on-chip
		communication standard assuming cooperative behavior
		among the manager modules AND an unsafe switching
		methodology (e.g., cut-through) is in use. Some
		switching methodologies may be susceptible to this
		weakness in modern on-chip multi-channel communication
		standards, such as the cut-through switching policy, a
		switching methodology for high performance commonly
		implemented at the interconnect level. In cut-through,
		a request is propagated independently on the receipt
		at th

e interconnect level of the corresponding
		data. If the manager module issuing a write request
		delays the provisioning of the corresponding data, the
		other manager modules experience delays in accessing
		the bus. Such delays are capable of generating denial
		of service.
Common_Consequences.Consequence.Scope: Availability
Common_Consequences.Consequence.Impact: DoS: Prevent Access
Common_Consequences.Consequence.Likelihood: High
Common_Consequences.Consequence.Note.xhtml:p: The technical impact could include
		Memory-access delays, I/O access delays, deadline
		miss, etc., The attacker can leverage this weakness to
		generate unbounded delays and denial of service (DoS)
		in the access of shared resources. The system
		interconnect might be left in an inconsistent state,
		requiring a partial or full reset of the network,
		according to the implementation. The scenario may
		play out as follows. The interconnect receives a write
		request from a controller initiator (e.g., sending the
		header to the interconnect for writing N words of
		data, with N ranging from 1 to the maximum burst
		length allowed). The interconnect then speculatively
		propagates the request to the target peripheral
		through the shared bus before the corresponding data
		are received at the interconnect. Here, the word
		"speculatively" refers to the fact that the
		interconnect propagates the request, assuming that the
		controller will at some point provide the data, thus
		releasing the use of the bus. This speculatively
		reserves the bus to the manager transaction issuer,
		which is left free to delay its data provisioning
		phase. This reserves the whole bus path between the
		initiator and the target peripheral until all of the
		words associated with the request are provided by the

controller. If the interconnect assumes a cooperative
		behavior from the controller, it is implicitly
		trusting that the controller will complete the
		transaction and release the bus for use from the other
		controllers. A malicious, faulty, or misbehaving
		manager module can generate a denial-of-service
		condition in preventing access to the write data link
		from all of the other managers in the system, and
		unboundedly inhibit the write access to one or
		multiple peripherals in the system (i.e., memories,
		I/Os, etc.).
Detection_Methods.Detection_Method[0].Method: Architecture or Design Review
Detection_Methods.Detection_Method[0].Description.xhtml:p: Instances of this issue can be detected by
		manual review of the switching policy implemented in
		the interconnect and the deployed on-chip
		communication standard.
Detection_Methods.Detection_Method[0].Effectiveness: Opportunistic
Detection_Methods.Detection_Method[0].Effectiveness_Notes.xhtml:p: Manual review requires to have a full
		description of the architecture of the
		interconnect. This information might not be available
		when a third-party interconnect is used.
Detection_Methods.Detection_Method[1].Method: Formal Verification
Detection_Methods.Detection_Method[1].Description.xhtml:p: Instances of this issue can be found in
		manager modules by using property-based verification
		specifically targeting the detection of stalls
		propagated to the shared resources
		[REF-1588].
Detection_Methods.Detection_Method[1].Effectiveness: High
Detection_Methods.Detection_Method[2].Method: Simulation / Emulation
Detection_Methods.Detection_Method[2].Description.xhtml:p: Instances of this issue can be found in
		simulation by synthetically generating stalls at the
		input of the interconnect and evaluating if

the
		interconnect propagates the stalls at the output or
		not.
Detection_Methods.Detection_Method[2].Effectiveness: Moderate
Detection_Methods.Detection_Method[2].Effectiveness_Notes.xhtml:p: Simulations should be capable of triggering
		the stalls. Not all of the Verification IP for on-chip
		communications might be capable of triggering this
		issue.
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation.Custom_Phase[0].@Domain: Hardware
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation.Custom_Phase[0].#text: Hardware Architecture
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation.Custom_Phase[1].@Domain: Hardware
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation.Custom_Phase[1].#text: Hardware Microarchitecture
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation.Description.xhtml:p: SoC architects can use a switching
		methodology stopping stalls from being propagated to
		the interconnect, such as Cut-and-Forward
		[REF-1585][REF-1587] or
		Store-and-Forward. Alternatively, a monitoring and
		recovery module can be added between the interconnect
		and each manager module to detect stalls introduced by
		the module and restore a safe state in the
		interconnect after a stall has been detected
		[REF-1586].
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation.Effectiveness: High
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation.Effectiveness_Notes.xhtml:p: The architect should evaluate which
		methodology better suits the target platform, trading
		off performance and resource consumption impact
		[REF-1585][REF-1586][REF-1587].
Demonstrative_Examples.Demonstrative_Example.Intro_Text.xhtml:p: In a system-on-chip, multiple hardware
		components may communicate with shared resources
		through an interconnect. A manager initiates
		transactions, while a target is a shared resource such
		as memory or a peripheral. A shared write path is the
		portion of the interconnect used by multiple managers

to send write data to the same target., To reduce buffering requirements and
		propagation latency, an interconnect may use
		cut-through switching. In protocols where the write
		request and corresponding write data are transferred
		independently, the interconnect can forward the
		request before all of the associated write data have
		arrived.
Demonstrative_Examples.Demonstrative_Example.Body_Text[0].xhtml:img.@src: /data/images/CWE-1476-cut-through.png
Demonstrative_Examples.Demonstrative_Example.Body_Text[0].xhtml:img.@alt: cut-through diagram
Demonstrative_Examples.Demonstrative_Example.Body_Text[1].xhtml:ul.xhtml:li: (a) Manager A issues a multi-word write
		  request., (b) The interconnect forwards the request
		  to the shared target before receiving all
		  corresponding write data. The shared write path is
		  reserved for Manager A until its data transfer
		  completes., (c) Manager A delays or stops sending the
		  remaining data. The transaction remains incomplete,
		  and the shared write path remains
		  reserved., (d) Manager B attempts to use the same shared path but cannot proceed
		  until Manager A completes the data transfer or a recovery mechanism
		  safely releases the path.
Demonstrative_Examples.Demonstrative_Example.Body_Text[1].xhtml:p: In these diagrams, "reserved" refers to the
		shared write path serving the target, rather than
		every operation or route to that target.
Demonstrative_Examples.Demonstrative_Example.Body_Text[2].xhtml:p: The interconnect reserves the shared
	      write path before the data required to complete the
	      transaction are available. In the problematic design
	      shown here, other managers cannot use that shared write
	      path until the corresponding data transfer
	      completes. Thus, the interconn

ect depends on Manager A
	      to continue making forward progress. If Manager A
	      stalls, the stall propagates into the shared portion of
	      the interconnect and prevents competing transactions
	      from using that shared write path.
Demonstrative_Examples.Demonstrative_Example.Body_Text[3].xhtml:p: One approach is store-and-forward switching the
		interconnect buffers the request and all corresponding
		write data before forwarding the request, preventing a
		manager's input-side stall from propagating into the
		shared write path. If Manager A delays or stops sending
		data, its incomplete transaction remains in the input
		buffer, and the shared write path remains available to
		transactions from other managers.
Demonstrative_Examples.Demonstrative_Example.Body_Text[4].xhtml:img.@src: /data/images/CWE-1476-store-and-forward-1.png
Demonstrative_Examples.Demonstrative_Example.Body_Text[4].xhtml:img.@alt: store-and-forward diagram
Demonstrative_Examples.Demonstrative_Example.Body_Text[5].xhtml:ul.xhtml:li: (a) Manager A issues a multi-word write
		  request., (b) The interconnect buffers the request
		  and waits for all corresponding write data. The
		  request has not been forwarded, and the shared write
		  path is not yet reserved for Manager A., (c) After all data have been received and
		  buffered, the interconnect forwards the request to
		  the shared target., (d) The interconnect forwards the buffered
		  data without waiting for additional data from
		  Manager A. Completion of the data transfer releases
		  the shared write path. The target completes the
		  write and returns a response through the
		  interconnect to Manager A.
Demonstrative_Examples.Demonstrative_Example.Body_Text[6].xhtml:p: Store-and-forward requires storage for an
		entire

transaction, increasing buffer capacity and
		hardware area. It also adds buffering latency because
		forwarding begins only after all corresponding data
		have arrived. [REF-1585]
Demonstrative_Examples.Demonstrative_Example.Body_Text[7].xhtml:img.@src: /data/images/CWE-1476-cut-and-forward-2.png
Demonstrative_Examples.Demonstrative_Example.Body_Text[7].xhtml:img.@alt: cut-and-forward diagram
Demonstrative_Examples.Demonstrative_Example.Body_Text[8].xhtml:ul.xhtml:li: (a) Manager A issues a four-word write
		  request., (b) The interconnect buffers the request
		  and begins receiving the corresponding write
		  data. The request has not been forwarded, so the
		  shared write path is not yet reserved for this
		  transaction., (c) After the first two words have been
		  buffered, the interconnect creates a two-word write
		  request and forwards it with the complete first
		  chunk to the shared target. While forwarding this
		  chunk, the interconnect can receive and buffer the
		  next two words., (d) After the remaining two words have
		  been buffered, the interconnect creates and forwards
		  a second two-word write transaction with the
		  complete second chunk., (e) The shared target completes the two
		  shorter transactions and returns a separate response
		  for each one., (f) The interconnect waits for both
		  responses, combines them into the single response
		  expected for the original transaction, and returns
		  that response to Manager A.
Demonstrative_Examples.Demonstrative_Example.Body_Text[9].xhtml:p: The shared write path is reserved only when a
		complete chunk is ready. If Manager A delays data for
		a later chunk, the incomplete chunk remains in the
		input buffer; the path is not held while waiting for
		those data and remains available to ot

her
		managers. Smaller chunks reduce buffering requirements
		and forwarding delay but increase target-side
		transaction and response overhead. Larger chunks
		reduce that overhead but require more buffering and
		increase the delay before forwarding
		begins. [REF-1585]
Demonstrative_Examples.Demonstrative_Example.Body_Text[10].xhtml:p: The behavior illustrated here has been
		demonstrated in AXI-based interconnects. The weakness
		is not inherently specific to AXI and can arise in
		other interconnect protocols with equivalent
		request/data separation, ordering,
		resource-commitment, and progress properties. The
		diagrams omit signal-level details to focus on the
		shared write path and transaction
		sequence. [REF-1585][REF-1586]
Demonstrative_Examples.Demonstrative_Example.Example_Code[0].@Nature: Attack
Demonstrative_Examples.Demonstrative_Example.Example_Code[0].xhtml:p: A faulty or malicious manager can delay or
		stop providing the remaining write data. If the
		interconnect does not enforce bounded progress or
		provide a recovery mechanism, the manager can hold the
		shared write path indefinitely and cause a denial of
		service for competing write transactions that require
		the same shared write path.
Demonstrative_Examples.Demonstrative_Example.Example_Code[1].@Nature: Good
Demonstrative_Examples.Demonstrative_Example.Example_Code[1].@Language: Other
Demonstrative_Examples.Demonstrative_Example.Example_Code[1].xhtml:p: The interconnect should avoid reserving the
		shared write path until the data needed to complete
		the forwarded transaction are available.
Demonstrative_Examples.Demonstrative_Example.Example_Code[2].@Nature: Good
Demonstrative_Examples.Demonstrative_Example.Example_Code[2].@Language: Other
Demonstrative_Examples.Demonstrative_Example.

Example_Code[2].xhtml:p: Cut-and-forward is a second preventive approach. It divides a
		transaction into smaller transactions and forwards each only after all
		data for that chunk have been buffered. Like store-and-forward, it
		prevents a manager's data-provisioning stall from reserving the shared
		write path. [REF-1585], Cut-and-forward applies the same principle at a smaller chunk
		granularity. In Figure 3, a four-word write is divided into two
		chunks of two words each. The interconnect creates the shorter
		transactions and combines their responses, so Manager A continues to
		issue and receive a response for the original transaction. [REF-1585]
Demonstrative_Examples.Demonstrative_Example.Example_Code[3].@Nature: Good
Demonstrative_Examples.Demonstrative_Example.Example_Code[3].@Language: Other
Demonstrative_Examples.Demonstrative_Example.Example_Code[3].xhtml:p: A watchdog with protocol-aware recovery is a third,
		separate mitigation approach. It limits the duration
		of a stall by restoring the shared path to a usable
		state. It does not prevent the stall from entering the
		shared path: other managers may remain blocked until
		detection and recovery complete. Detection alone does
		not release the path. [REF-1586]
Observed_Examples.Observed_Example.Reference: [REF-1586]
Observed_Examples.Observed_Example.Description: Certain commercial AXI interconnect IPs
	      could allow a manager to cause bus stalls.

Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[0].Description: Developers should anticipate that leading characters will be injected/removed/manipulated in the input vectors of their product. Use an appropriate combination of denylists and allowlists to ensure only valid, expected and appropriate input is processed by the system.
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[1].@Mitigation_ID: MIT-5
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[1].Phase: Implementation
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[1].Strategy: Input Validation
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[1].Description.xhtml:p: Assume all input is malicious. Use an "accept known good" input validation strategy, i.e., use a list of acceptable inputs that strictly conform to specifications. Reject any input that does not strictly conform to specifications, or transform it into something that does., When performing input validation, consider all potentially relevant properties, including length, type of input, the

full range of acceptable values, missing or extra inputs, syntax, consistency across related fields, and conformance to business rules. As an example of business rule logic, "boat" may be syntactically valid because it only contains alphanumeric characters, but it is not valid if the input is only expected to contain colors such as "red" or "blue.", Do not rely exclusively on looking for malicious or malformed inputs. This is likely to miss at least one undesirable input, especially if the code's environment changes. This can give attackers enough room to bypass the intended validation. However, denylists can be useful for detecting potential attacks or determining which inputs are so malformed that they should be rejected outright.
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[2].@Mitigation_ID: MIT-28
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[2].Phase: Implementation
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[2].Strategy: Output Encoding
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[2].Description: While it is risky to use dynamically-generated query strings, code, or commands that mix control and data together, sometimes it may be unavoidable. Properly quote arguments and escape any special characters within those arguments. The most conservative approach is to escape or filter all characters that do not pass an extremely strict allowlist (such as everything that is not alphanumeric or white space). If some special characters are still needed, such as white space, wrap each argument in quotes after the escaping/filtering step. Be careful of argument injection (CWE-88).
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[3].@Mitigation_ID: MIT-20
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[3].Phase: Implementation
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[3].Strategy: Input Validation
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[3].Description: Inputs should be

decoded and canonicalized to the application's current internal representation before being validated (CWE-180). Make sure that the application does not decode the same input twice (CWE-174). Such errors could be used to bypass allowlist validation schemes by introducing dangerous inputs after they have been checked.

Detection_Methods.Detection_Method.@Detection_Method_ID: DM-14
Detection_Methods.Detection_Method.Method: Automated Static Analysis
Detection_Methods.Detection_Method.Description: Automated static analysis, commonly referred to as Static Application Security Testing (SAST), can find some instances of this weakness by analyzing source code (or binary/compiled code) without having to execute it. Typically, this is done by building a model of data flow and control flow, then searching for potentially-vulnerable patterns that connect "sources" (origins of input) with "sinks" (destinations where the data interacts with external components, a lower layer such as the OS, etc.)
Detection_Methods.Detection_Method.Effectiveness: High
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[0].@Mitigation_ID: MIT-46
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[0].Phase: Architecture and Design
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[0].Strategy: Separation of Privilege
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[0].Description.xhtml:p: Compartmentalize the system to have "safe" areas where trust boundaries can be unambiguously drawn. Do not allow sensitive data to go outside of the trust boundary and always be careful when interfacing with a compartment outside of the safe area., Ensure that appropriate compartmentalization is built into the system design, and the compartmentalization allows for and reinforces privilege separation functionality. Architects and designers should rely on the principle of least privilege to decide the appropriate time to use privileges and the time to drop privileges.
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[1].Phase: Implementation, Architecture and Design
Potential_Mitigations.M

itigation[1].Description: Because setting manipulation covers a diverse set of functions, any attempt at illustrating it will inevitably be incomplete. Rather than searching for a tight-knit relationship between the functions addressed in the setting manipulation category, take a step back and consider the sorts of system values that an attacker should not be allowed to control.
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[2].Phase: Implementation, Architecture and Design
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[2].Description: In general, do not allow user-provided or otherwise untrusted data to control sensitive values. The leverage that an attacker gains by controlling these values is not always immediately obvious, but do not underestimate the creativity of the attacker.

@Name: Improper Neutralization of Escape, Meta, or Control Sequences
@Abstraction: Variant

Description: The product receives input from an upstream component, but it does not neutralize or incorrectly neutralizes special elements that could be interpreted as escape, meta, or control character sequences when they are sent to a downstream component.

Alternate_Terms.Alternate_Term.Term: ANSI injection
Alternate_Terms.Alternate_Term.Description: injection of ANSI escape sequences.
Modes_Of_Introduction.Introduction[0].Phase: Build and Compilation
Modes_Of_Introduction.Introduction[0].Note: During LLM training, escape sequences may be
               assigned within token entry values.
Modes_Of_Introduction.Introduction[1].Phase: Implementation
Modes_Of_Introduction.Introduction[1].Note: Interactive command line interfaces have become
               more commonplace with growing system administration
               needs and human-friendly TUIs (text-based user
               interfaces); logging user-generated values into the
               terminal into one of these sessions is no longer
               safe.
Modes_Of_Introduction.Introduction[2].Phase: Implementation
Modes_Of_Introduction.Introduction[2].Note: REALIZATION: This weakness is ca

used during implementation of an architectural security tactic.
Common_Consequences.Consequence.Scope: Integrity
Common_Consequences.Consequence.Impact: Execute Unauthorized Code or Commands, Hide Activities, Unexpected State
Common_Consequences.Consequence.Note: ANSI escape codes can be used for low-severity
	       attacks such as changing the color of console output,
	       but they can also be used to arbitrarily move the
	       cursor, clear the screen, and make fake prompts inside
	       the interactive CLI via malicious user input. In some
	       contexts - depending on the functionality of the
	       terminal in use - ANSI escape codes can be used to
	       execute arbitrary code.
Detection_Methods.Detection_Method.@Detection_Method_ID: DM-14
Detection_Methods.Detection_Method.Method: Automated Static Analysis
Detection_Methods.Detection_Method.Description: Automated static analysis, commonly referred to as Static Application Security Testing (SAST), can find some instances of this weakness by analyzing source code (or binary/compiled code) without having to execute it. Typically, this is done by building a model of data flow and control flow, then searching for potentially-vulnerable patterns that connect "sources" (origins of input) with "sinks" (destinations where the data interacts with external components, a lower layer such as the OS, etc.)
Detection_Methods.Detection_Method.Effectiveness: High
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[0].Description: Developers should anticipate that escape, meta and control characters/sequences will be injected/removed/manipulated in the input vectors of their product. Use an appropriate combination of denylists and allowlists to ensure only valid, expected and appropriate input is processed by the system.
Potential_Mitigat

ions.Mitigation[1].@Mitigation_ID: MIT-5
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[1].Phase: Implementation
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[1].Strategy: Input Validation
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[1].Description.xhtml:p: Assume all input is malicious. Use an "accept known good" input validation strategy, i.e., use a list of acceptable inputs that strictly conform to specifications. Reject any input that does not strictly conform to specifications, or transform it into something that does., When performing input validation, consider all potentially relevant properties, including length, type of input, the full range of acceptable values, missing or extra inputs, syntax, consistency across related fields, and conformance to business rules. As an example of business rule logic, "boat" may be syntactically valid because it only contains alphanumeric characters, but it is not valid if the input is only expected to contain colors such as "red" or "blue.", Do not rely exclusively on looking for malicious or malformed inputs. This is likely to miss at least one undesirable input, especially if the code's environment changes. This can give attackers enough room to bypass the intended validation. However, denylists can be useful for detecting potential attacks or determining which inputs are so malformed that they should be rejected outright.
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[2].@Mitigation_ID: MIT-28
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[2].Phase: Implementation
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[2].Strategy: Output Encoding
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[2].Description: While it is risky to use dynamically-generated query strings, code, or commands that mix control and data together, sometimes it may be unavoidable. Properly quote arguments and escape any special characters within thos

e arguments. The most conservative approach is to escape or filter all characters that do not pass an extremely strict allowlist (such as everything that is not alphanumeric or white space). If some special characters are still needed, such as white space, wrap each argument in quotes after the escaping/filtering step. Be careful of argument injection (CWE-88).
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[3].@Mitigation_ID: MIT-20
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[3].Phase: Implementation
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[3].Strategy: Input Validation
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[3].Description: Inputs should be decoded and canonicalized to the application's current internal representation before being validated (CWE-180). Make sure that the application does not decode the same input twice (CWE-174). Such errors could be used to bypass allowlist validation schemes by introducing dangerous inputs after they have been checked.
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[4].Phase: Implementation
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[4].Description: When using output from an LLM, neutralize
              or strip escape codes before redirecting output to the
              terminal or other rendering engine that would process
              the codes. The neutralization could require that the
              character be printable and/or allowable whitespace, such
              as a carriage return or newline. Be deliberate about
              what to allow.
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[4].Effectiveness: High
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[4].Effectiveness_Notes: By restricting output to only printable
	      characters, this effectively removes any escape codes.
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[5].Phase: Build and Compilation
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[5].Description: When using an LLM: dur

ing tokenizer
              training, suppress escape codes from the tokenizer's
              vocabulary. Depending on context, this could be
              accomplished by removing the codes from input to the
              tokenizer, or removing the map from the string to its
              token ID. It is generally unlikely that this removal
              would adversely affect the quality or correctness of
              what is generated, e.g. advice requests for terminal
              settings to change colors.
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[5].Effectiveness: Limited
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[5].Effectiveness_Notes: This could raise the exploitation
	      effort for an adversary, but the adversary might still
	      be able to get string together multiple tokens in order
	      to form the escape code.
Demonstrative_Examples.Demonstrative_Example.Intro_Text: Consider a situation in which an AI agent
	     uses LLM output based on training data from untrusted
	     sources.
Demonstrative_Examples.Demonstrative_Example.Body_Text: Suppose an attacker is able to inject input
	     into the training data that is used by the LLM. If a
	     person is using a terminal emulator to interact with the
	     LLM on the command line, if the output contains escape
	     codes, then the emulator might act on those codes, e.g.,
	     to change color, flash text, or (in some cases) leak
	     sensitive information or execute code. In one documented
	     case, a terminal would handle an OSC (Operating System
	     Command) for setting the working directory by processing
	     a file:// URL in a way that could perform a DNS lookup
	     for an adversary-controlled domain, leading to an
	     information leak [REF-1526].

Notes.Note.#text: As of CWE 4.20: while
            exploitation and research interest in ANSI escape codes
            (and other terminal sequences) was popular in the early
            2000's [REF-1527] - and known as an attack vector going
            back to at least 1994 [REF-1532] - there has been renewed
            interest in this type of injection as new attack vectors
            have arrived (e.g., from LLM output, or CLIs that were not
            based on OS sessions).

s, including length, type of input, the full range of acceptable values, missing or extra inputs, syntax, consistency across related fields, and conformance to business rules. As an example of business rule logic, "boat" may be syntactically valid because it only contains alphanumeric characters, but it is not valid if the input is only expected to contain colors such as "red" or "blue.", Do not rely exclusively on looking for malicious or malformed inputs. This is likely to miss at least one undesirable input, especially if the code's environment changes. This can give attackers enough room to bypass the intended validation. However, denylists can be useful for detecting potential attacks or determining which inputs are so malformed that they should be rejected outright.

Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[2].Description: While it is risky to use dynamically-generated query strings, code, or commands that mix control and data together, sometimes it may be unavoidable. The most conservative approach is to escape or filter all characters that do not pass an extremely strict allowlist (such as everything that is not alphanumeric or white space). If some special characters are still needed, such as white space, wrap each argument in quotes after the escaping/filtering step. Be careful of argument injection (CWE-88).

Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[1].Phase: Implementation
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[1].Strategy: Input Validation
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[1].Description.xhtml:p: Assume all input is malicious. Use an "accept known good" input validation strategy, i.e., use a list of acceptable inputs that strictly conform to specifications. Reject any input that does not strictly conform to specifications, or transform it into something that does., When performing input validation, consider all poten

tially relevant properties, including length, type of input, the full range of acceptable values, missing or extra inputs, syntax, consistency across related fields, and conformance to business rules. As an example of business rule logic, "boat" may be syntactically valid because it only contains alphanumeric characters, but it is not valid if the input is only expected to contain colors such as "red" or "blue.", Do not rely exclusively on looking for malicious or malformed inputs. This is likely to miss at least one undesirable input, especially if the code's environment changes. This can give attackers enough room to bypass the intended validation. However, denylists can be useful for detecting potential attacks or determining which inputs are so malformed that they should be rejected outright.
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[2].@Mitigation_ID: MIT-28
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[2].Phase: Implementation
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[2].Strategy: Output Encoding
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[2].Description: While it is risky to use dynamically-generated query strings, code, or commands that mix control and data together, sometimes it may be unavoidable. Properly quote arguments and escape any special characters within those arguments. The most conservative approach is to escape or filter all characters that do not pass an extremely strict allowlist (such as everything that is not alphanumeric or white space). If some special characters are still needed, such as white space, wrap each argument in quotes after the escaping/filtering step. Be careful of argument injection (CWE-88).

Detection_Methods.Detection_Method.@Detection_Method_ID: DM-14
Detection_Methods.Detection_Method.Method: Automated Static Analysis
Detection_Methods.Detection_Method.Description: Automated static analysis, commonly referred to as Static Application Security Testing (SAST), can find some instances of this weakness by analyzing source code (or binary/compiled code) without having to execute it. Typically, this is done by building a model of data flow and control flow, then searching for potentially-vulnerable patterns that connect "sources" (origins of input) with "sinks" (destinations where the data interacts with external components, a lower layer such as the OS, etc.)
Detection_Methods.Detection_Method.Effectiveness

: High
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[0].Description: Developers should anticipate that wildcard or matching elements will be injected/removed/manipulated in the input vectors of their product. Use an appropriate combination of denylists and allowlists to ensure only valid, expected and appropriate input is processed by the system.
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[1].@Mitigation_ID: MIT-5
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[1].Phase: Implementation
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[1].Strategy: Input Validation
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[1].Description.xhtml:p: Assume all input is malicious. Use an "accept known good" input validation strategy, i.e., use a list of acceptable inputs that strictly conform to specifications. Reject any input that does not strictly conform to specifications, or transform it into something that does., When performing input validation, consider all potentially relevant properties, including length, type of input, the full range of acceptable values, missing or extra inputs, syntax, consistency across related fields, and conformance to business rules. As an example of business rule logic, "boat" may be syntactically valid because it only contains alphanumeric characters, but it is not valid if the input is only expected to contain colors such as "red" or "blue.", Do not rely exclusively on looking for malicious or malformed inputs. This is likely to miss at least one undesirable input, especially if the code's environment changes. This can give attackers enough room to bypass the intended validation. However, denylists can be useful for detecting potential attacks or determining which inputs are so malformed that they should be rejected outright.
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[2].@Mitigation_ID: MIT-28
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[2]

.Phase: Implementation
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[2].Strategy: Output Encoding
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[2].Description: While it is risky to use dynamically-generated query strings, code, or commands that mix control and data together, sometimes it may be unavoidable. Properly quote arguments and escape any special characters within those arguments. The most conservative approach is to escape or filter all characters that do not pass an extremely strict allowlist (such as everything that is not alphanumeric or white space). If some special characters are still needed, such as white space, wrap each argument in quotes after the escaping/filtering step. Be careful of argument injection (CWE-88).

Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[3].Phase: Implementation
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[3].Strategy: Input Validation
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[3].Description: Inputs should be decoded and canonicalized to the application's current internal representation before being validated (CWE-180). Make sure that the application does not decode the same input twice (CWE-174). Such errors could be used to bypass allowlist validation schemes by introducing dangerous inputs after they have been checked.

Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[1].Strategy: Input Validation
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[1].Description.xhtml:p: Assume all input is malicious. Use an "accept known good" input validation strategy, i.e., use a list of acceptable inputs that strictly conform to specifications. Reject any inp

ut that does not strictly conform to specifications, or transform it into something that does., When performing input validation, consider all potentially relevant properties, including length, type of input, the full range of acceptable values, missing or extra inputs, syntax, consistency across related fields, and conformance to business rules. As an example of business rule logic, "boat" may be syntactically valid because it only contains alphanumeric characters, but it is not valid if the input is only expected to contain colors such as "red" or "blue.", Do not rely exclusively on looking for malicious or malformed inputs. This is likely to miss at least one undesirable input, especially if the code's environment changes. This can give attackers enough room to bypass the intended validation. However, denylists can be useful for detecting potential attacks or determining which inputs are so malformed that they should be rejected outright.
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[2].@Mitigation_ID: MIT-28
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[2].Phase: Implementation
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[2].Strategy: Output Encoding
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[2].Description: While it is risky to use dynamically-generated query strings, code, or commands that mix control and data together, sometimes it may be unavoidable. Properly quote arguments and escape any special characters within those arguments. The most conservative approach is to escape or filter all characters that do not pass an extremely strict allowlist (such as everything that is not alphanumeric or white space). If some special characters are still needed, such as white space, wrap each argument in quotes after the escaping/filtering step. Be careful of argument injection (CWE-88).

Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[0].Description: Developers should anticipate that special elements will be injected/removed/manipulated in the input vectors of their software system. Use an appropriate combination of denylists and allowlists to ensure only valid, expected and appropriate input is processed by the system.
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[1].@Mitigation_ID: MIT-5
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[1].Phase: Implementation
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[1].Strategy: Input Validation
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[1].Description.xhtml:p: Assume all input is malicious. Use an "accept known good" input validation strategy, i.e., use a list of acceptable inputs that strictly conform to specifications. Reject any input that does not strictly conform to specifications, or transform it into something that does., When performing input validation, consider all potentially relevant propertie

s, including length, type of input, the full range of acceptable values, missing or extra inputs, syntax, consistency across related fields, and conformance to business rules. As an example of business rule logic, "boat" may be syntactically valid because it only contains alphanumeric characters, but it is not valid if the input is only expected to contain colors such as "red" or "blue.", Do not rely exclusively on looking for malicious or malformed inputs. This is likely to miss at least one undesirable input, especially if the code's environment changes. This can give attackers enough room to bypass the intended validation. However, denylists can be useful for detecting potential attacks or determining which inputs are so malformed that they should be rejected outright.
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[2].@Mitigation_ID: MIT-28
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[2].Phase: Implementation
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[2].Strategy: Output Encoding
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[2].Description: While it is risky to use dynamically-generated query strings, code, or commands that mix control and data together, sometimes it may be unavoidable. Properly quote arguments and escape any special characters within those arguments. The most conservative approach is to escape or filter all characters that do not pass an extremely strict allowlist (such as everything that is not alphanumeric or white space). If some special characters are still needed, such as white space, wrap each argument in quotes after the escaping/filtering step. Be careful of argument injection (CWE-88).
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[3].@Mitigation_ID: MIT-20
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[3].Phase: Implementation
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[3].Strategy: Input Validation

Notes.Note[2].@Type: Research Gap
Notes.Note[2].#text: Customized languages and grammars, even those that are specific to a particular product, are potential sources of weaknesses that are related to special elements. Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[0].Description: Developers should anticipate that multiple leading special elements will be injected/removed/manipulated in the input vectors of their product. Use an appropriate combination of denylists and allowlists to ensure only valid, expected and appropriate input is processed by the system.
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[1].@Mitigation_ID: MIT-5
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[1].Phase: Implementation
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[1].Strategy: Input Validation
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[1].Description.xhtml:p: Assume all input is malicious. Use an "accept known good" input validation strategy, i.e., use a list of acceptable inputs that strictly conform t

o specifications. Reject any input that does not strictly conform to specifications, or transform it into something that does., When performing input validation, consider all potentially relevant properties, including length, type of input, the full range of acceptable values, missing or extra inputs, syntax, consistency across related fields, and conformance to business rules. As an example of business rule logic, "boat" may be syntactically valid because it only contains alphanumeric characters, but it is not valid if the input is only expected to contain colors such as "red" or "blue.", Do not rely exclusively on looking for malicious or malformed inputs. This is likely to miss at least one undesirable input, especially if the code's environment changes. This can give attackers enough room to bypass the intended validation. However, denylists can be useful for detecting potential attacks or determining which inputs are so malformed that they should be rejected outright.
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[2].@Mitigation_ID: MIT-28
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[2].Phase: Implementation
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[2].Strategy: Output Encoding
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[2].Description: While it is risky to use dynamically-generated query strings, code, or commands that mix control and data together, sometimes it may be unavoidable. Properly quote arguments and escape any special characters within those arguments. The most conservative approach is to escape or filter all characters that do not pass an extremely strict allowlist (such as everything that is not alphanumeric or white space). If some special characters are still needed, such as white space, wrap each argument in quotes after the escaping/filtering step. Be careful of argument injection (CWE-88).

otential_Mitigations.Mitigation[3].@Mitigation_ID: MIT-20
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[3].Phase: Implementation
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[3].Strategy: Input Validation
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[3].Description: Inputs should be decoded and canonicalized to the application's current internal representation before being validated (CWE-180). Make sure that the application does not decode the same input twice (CWE-174). Such errors could be used to bypass allowlist validation schemes by introducing dangerous inputs after they have been checked.

Modes_Of_Introduction.Introduction.Phase: Implementation
Common_Consequences.Consequence.Scope: Integrity
Common_Consequences.Consequence.Impact: Unexpected State, Varies by Context
Common_Consequences.Consequence.Note: As data is parsed, an injected element may cause the process to take unexpected actions.
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[0].Description: Developers should anticipate that internal special elements will be injected/removed/manipulated in the input vectors of their product. Use an appropriate combination of denylists and allowlists to ensure only valid, expected and appropriate input is processed by the system.
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[1].@Mitigation_ID: MIT-5
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[1].Phase: Implementation
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[1].Strategy: Input Validation
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[1].Description.xhtml:p: Assume all input is malicious. Use an "accept known good" input validation strategy, i.e., use a list of acceptable inputs that strictly conform to specifications. Reject

any input that does not strictly conform to specifications, or transform it into something that does., When performing input validation, consider all potentially relevant properties, including length, type of input, the full range of acceptable values, missing or extra inputs, syntax, consistency across related fields, and conformance to business rules. As an example of business rule logic, "boat" may be syntactically valid because it only contains alphanumeric characters, but it is not valid if the input is only expected to contain colors such as "red" or "blue.", Do not rely exclusively on looking for malicious or malformed inputs. This is likely to miss at least one undesirable input, especially if the code's environment changes. This can give attackers enough room to bypass the intended validation. However, denylists can be useful for detecting potential attacks or determining which inputs are so malformed that they should be rejected outright.
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[2].@Mitigation_ID: MIT-28
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[2].Phase: Implementation
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[2].Strategy: Output Encoding
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[2].Description: While it is risky to use dynamically-generated query strings, code, or commands that mix control and data together, sometimes it may be unavoidable. Properly quote arguments and escape any special characters within those arguments. The most conservative approach is to escape or filter all characters that do not pass an extremely strict allowlist (such as everything that is not alphanumeric or white space). If some special characters are still needed, such as white space, wrap each argument in quotes after the escaping/filtering step. Be careful of argument injection (CWE-88).

igation[3].@Mitigation_ID: MIT-20

Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[3].Strategy: Input Validation

Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[0].Description: Developers should anticipate that special elements will be removed in the input vectors of their product. Use an appropriate combination of denylists and allowlists to ensure only valid, expected and appropriate input is processed by the system.
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[1].@Mitigation_ID: MIT-5
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[1].Phase: Implementation
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[1].Strategy: Input Validation
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[1].Description.xhtml:p: Assume all input is malicious. Use an "accept known good" input validation strategy, i.e., use a list of acceptable inputs that strictly conform to specifications. Reject any input that does not strictly conform to specifications, or transform it into s

omething that does., When performing input validation, consider all potentially relevant properties, including length, type of input, the full range of acceptable values, missing or extra inputs, syntax, consistency across related fields, and conformance to business rules. As an example of business rule logic, "boat" may be syntactically valid because it only contains alphanumeric characters, but it is not valid if the input is only expected to contain colors such as "red" or "blue.", Do not rely exclusively on looking for malicious or malformed inputs. This is likely to miss at least one undesirable input, especially if the code's environment changes. This can give attackers enough room to bypass the intended validation. However, denylists can be useful for detecting potential attacks or determining which inputs are so malformed that they should be rejected outright.

Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[0].Description: Developers should anticipate that inconsistent special elements will be injected/manipulated in the input vectors of their product. Use an appropriate combination of denylists and allowlists to ensure only valid, expected and appropriate input is processed by the system.
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[1].@Mitigation_ID: MIT-5
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[1].Phase: Implementation
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[1].Strategy: Input Validation
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[1].Description.xht

ml:p: Assume all input is malicious. Use an "accept known good" input validation strategy, i.e., use a list of acceptable inputs that strictly conform to specifications. Reject any input that does not strictly conform to specifications, or transform it into something that does., When performing input validation, consider all potentially relevant properties, including length, type of input, the full range of acceptable values, missing or extra inputs, syntax, consistency across related fields, and conformance to business rules. As an example of business rule logic, "boat" may be syntactically valid because it only contains alphanumeric characters, but it is not valid if the input is only expected to contain colors such as "red" or "blue.", Do not rely exclusively on looking for malicious or malformed inputs. This is likely to miss at least one undesirable input, especially if the code's environment changes. This can give attackers enough room to bypass the intended validation. However, denylists can be useful for detecting potential attacks or determining which inputs are so malformed that they should be rejected outright.
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[2].@Mitigation_ID: MIT-20
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[2].Phase: Implementation
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[2].Strategy: Input Validation
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[2].Description: Inputs should be decoded and canonicalized to the application's current internal representation before being validated (CWE-180). Make sure that the application does not decode the same input twice (CWE-174). Such errors could be used to bypass allowlist validation schemes by introducing dangerous inputs after they have been checked.

Modes_Of_Introduction.Introduction.Phase: Implementation
Modes_Of_Introduction.Introduction.Note: Null termination errors frequently occur in two different ways. An off-by-one error could cause a null to be written out of bounds, leading to an overflow. Or, a program could use a strncpy() function call incorrectly, which prevents a null terminator from being added at all. Other scenarios are possible.
Likelihood_Of_Exploit: Medium
Common_Consequences.Consequence[0].Scope: Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability
Common_Consequences.Consequence[0].Impact: Read Memory, Execute Unauthorized Code or Commands
Common_Consequences.Consequence[0].Note: The case of an omitted null character is the most dangerous of the possible issues. This will almost certainly result in information disclosure, and possibly a buffer overflow condition, which may be exploited to execute arbitrary code.
Common_Consequences.Consequence[1].Scope: Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability
Common_Consequences.Consequence[1].Impact: DoS: Crash, Exit, or Restart, Read Memory, DoS: Resource Consumption (CPU), DoS: Resource Consumption (Memory)
Common_Consequences.Consequence[1].Note: If a null character is omitted from a string, then most string-copying functions will read data until they locate a null character, even outside of t

he intended boundaries of the string. This could: cause a crash due to a segmentation fault cause sensitive adjacent memory to be copied and sent to an outsider trigger a buffer overflow when the copy is being written to a fixed-size buffer.
Common_Consequences.Consequence[2].Scope: Integrity, Availability
Common_Consequences.Consequence[2].Impact: Modify Memory, DoS: Crash, Exit, or Restart
Common_Consequences.Consequence[2].Note: Misplaced null characters may result in any number of security problems. The biggest issue is a subset of buffer overflow, and write-what-where conditions, where data corruption occurs from the writing of a null character over valid data, or even instructions. A randomly placed null character may put the system into an undefined state, and therefore make it prone to crashing. A misplaced null character may corrupt other data in memory.
Common_Consequences.Consequence[3].Scope: Integrity, Confidentiality, Availability, Access Control, Other
Common_Consequences.Consequence[3].Impact: Alter Execution Logic, Execute Unauthorized Code or Commands
Common_Consequences.Consequence[3].Note: Should the null character corrupt the process flow, or affect a flag controlling access, it may lead to logical errors which allow for the execution of arbitrary code.
Detection_Methods.Detection_Method.@Detection_Method_ID: DM-14
Detection_Methods.Detection_Method.Method: Automated Static Analysis
Detection_Methods.Detection_Method.Description: Automated static analysis, commonly referred to as Static Application Security Testing (SAST), can find some instances of this weakness by analyzing source code (or binary/compiled code) without having to execute it. Typically, this is done by building a model of data flow and control flow, then searching for potentially-vu

lnerable patterns that connect "sources" (origins of input) with "sinks" (destinations where the data interacts with external components, a lower layer such as the OS, etc.)
Detection_Methods.Detection_Method.Effectiveness: High
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[0].Phase: Requirements
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[0].Description: Use a language that is not susceptible to these issues. However, be careful of null byte interaction errors (CWE-626) with lower-level constructs that may be written in a language that is susceptible.
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[1].Phase: Implementation
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[1].Description: Ensure that all string functions used are understood fully as to how they append null characters. Also, be wary of off-by-one errors when appending nulls to the end of strings.
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[2].Phase: Implementation
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[2].Description: If performance constraints permit, special code can be added that validates null-termination of string buffers, this is a rather naive and error-prone solution.
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[3].Phase: Implementation
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[3].Description: Switch to bounded string manipulation functions. Inspect buffer lengths involved in the buffer overrun trace reported with the defect.
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[4].Phase: Implementation
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[4].Description: Add code that fills buffers with nulls (however, the length of buffers still needs to be inspected, to ensure that the non null-terminated string is not written at the physical end of the buffer).
Demonstrative_Examples.Demonstrative_Example[0].Intro_Text: The following code reads from cfgfile and copies the input into inputbuf using strcpy(). The code mistakenl

y assumes that inputbuf will always contain a NULL terminator.
Demonstrative_Examples.Demonstrative_Example[0].Example_Code.@Nature: Bad
Demonstrative_Examples.Demonstrative_Example[0].Example_Code.@Language: C
Demonstrative_Examples.Demonstrative_Example[0].Example_Code.xhtml:div.xhtml:br: null, null, null, null, null, null
Demonstrative_Examples.Demonstrative_Example[0].Example_Code.xhtml:div.#text: #define MAXLEN 1024...char *pathbuf[MAXLEN];...read(cfgfile,inputbuf,MAXLEN); //does not null terminatestrcpy(pathbuf,inputbuf); //requires null terminated input...
Demonstrative_Examples.Demonstrative_Example[0].Body_Text: The code above will behave correctly if the data read from cfgfile is null terminated on disk as expected. But if an attacker is able to modify this input so that it does not contain the expected NULL character, the call to strcpy() will continue copying from memory until it encounters an arbitrary NULL character. This will likely overflow the destination buffer and, if the attacker can control the contents of memory immediately following inputbuf, can leave the application susceptible to a buffer overflow attack.
Demonstrative_Examples.Demonstrative_Example[1].Intro_Text: In the following code, readlink() expands the name of a symbolic link stored in pathname and puts the absolute path into buf. The length of the resulting value is then calculated using strlen().
Demonstrative_Examples.Demonstrative_Example[1].Example_Code.@Nature: Bad
Demonstrative_Examples.Demonstrative_Example[1].Example_Code.@Language: C
Demonstrative_Examples.Demonstrative_Example[1].Example_Code.xhtml:div.xhtml:br: null, null, null, null
Demonstrative_Examples.Demonstrative_Example[1].Example_Code.xhtml:div.#text: char buf[MAXPATH];...readlink(pathname, buf, MAXPATH);int length =

strlen(buf);...
Demonstrative_Examples.Demonstrative_Example[1].Body_Text: The code above will not always behave correctly as readlink() does not append a NULL byte to buf. Readlink() will stop copying characters once the maximum size of buf has been reached to avoid overflowing the buffer, this will leave the value buf not NULL terminated. In this situation, strlen() will continue traversing memory until it encounters an arbitrary NULL character further on down the stack, resulting in a length value that is much larger than the size of string. Readlink() does return the number of bytes copied, but when this return value is the same as stated buf size (in this case MAXPATH), it is impossible to know whether the pathname is precisely that many bytes long, or whether readlink() has truncated the name to avoid overrunning the buffer. In testing, vulnerabilities like this one might not be caught because the unused contents of buf and the memory immediately following it may be NULL, thereby causing strlen() to appear as if it is behaving correctly.
Demonstrative_Examples.Demonstrative_Example[2].Intro_Text: While the following example is not exploitable, it provides a good example of how nulls can be omitted or misplaced, even when "safe" functions are used:
Demonstrative_Examples.Demonstrative_Example[2].Example_Code.@Nature: Bad
Demonstrative_Examples.Demonstrative_Example[2].Example_Code.@Language: C
Demonstrative_Examples.Demonstrative_Example[2].Example_Code.xhtml:div.xhtml:br: null, null, null
Demonstrative_Examples.Demonstrative_Example[2].Example_Code.xhtml:div.xhtml:div.@style: margin-left:1em;
Demonstrative_Examples.Demonstrative_Example[2].Example_Code.xhtml:div.xhtml:div.xhtml:div.xhtml:br: null, null, null, null, null, null
Demonstrative_Examples.Demonstrative_

Example[2].Example_Code.xhtml:div.xhtml:div.xhtml:div.#text: char longString[] = "String signifying nothing";char shortString[16];
                           strncpy(shortString, longString, 16);printf("The last character in shortString is: %c (%1$x)\n", shortString[15]);return (0);
Demonstrative_Examples.Demonstrative_Example[2].Example_Code.xhtml:div.#text: #include <stdio.h>#include <string.h>
                     int main() {}
Demonstrative_Examples.Demonstrative_Example[2].Body_Text: The above code gives the following output: "The last character in shortString is: n (6e)". So, the shortString array does not end in a NULL character, even though the "safe" string function strncpy() was used. The reason is that strncpy() does not implicitly add a NULL character at the end of the string when the source is equal in length or longer than the provided size.

Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[0].Phase: Implementation
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[0].Strategy: Input Validation
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[0].Description.xhtml:p: Assume all input is malicious. Use an "accept known good" input validation strategy, i.e., use a list of acceptable inputs that strictly conform to specifications. Reject any input that does not strictly conform to sp

ecifications, or transform it into something that does., When performing input validation, consider all potentially relevant properties, including length, type of input, the full range of acceptable values, missing or extra inputs, syntax, consistency across related fields, and conformance to business rules. As an example of business rule logic, "boat" may be syntactically valid because it only contains alphanumeric characters, but it is not valid if the input is only expected to contain colors such as "red" or "blue.", Do not rely exclusively on looking for malicious or malformed inputs. This is likely to miss at least one undesirable input, especially if the code's environment changes. This can give attackers enough room to bypass the intended validation. However, denylists can be useful for detecting potential attacks or determining which inputs are so malformed that they should be rejected outright.
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[1].@Mitigation_ID: MIT-28
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[1].Phase: Implementation
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[1].Strategy: Output Encoding
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[1].Description: While it is risky to use dynamically-generated query strings, code, or commands that mix control and data together, sometimes it may be unavoidable. Properly quote arguments and escape any special characters within those arguments. The most conservative approach is to escape or filter all characters that do not pass an extremely strict allowlist (such as everything that is not alphanumeric or white space). If some special characters are still needed, such as white space, wrap each argument in quotes after the escaping/filtering step. Be careful of argument injection (CWE-88).
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[2].@Mitigation_ID: MIT-20
Potential_Mit

igations.Mitigation[2].Phase: Implementation
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[2].Strategy: Input Validation
Potential_Mitigations.Mitigation[2].Description: Inputs should be decoded and canonicalized to the application's current internal representation before being validated (CWE-180). Make sure that the application does not decode the same input twice (CWE-174). Such errors could be used to bypass allowlist validation schemes by introducing dangerous inputs after they have been checked.
